sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the colors, shapes, and directions of the piece carry the mood its message calls for?** No. The text is about lanterns at dusk, hundreds of paper boats on the river, a brass band, a pie contest and gulls. The page is plain black serif text on white, set in three even columns with thin grey rules, and the bottom ~40% (y ≈ 470–800) is empty. Nothing in its colour, shape or direction hints at light, water, evening or fun. It reads like a council notice or the minutes of a meeting, so the viewer gets the facts but none of the pull to go. Itten (*The Art of Color*): colour temperature and value should match the feeling of the subject, and here they don't. The fix: let one strong visual idea about lights on the water carry the mood. That could be warm lantern colours against a dark evening ground, or a single image of the boats or lanterns, with the empty lower area used for it. Taste, backed by Itten. Weight: major for a festival promotion, because the piece has to make people want to come as well as inform them.
2. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears?** No. The three text columns are one set of matching elements, but the middle column's first line sits about 14 px lower than the other two (y ≈ 160 against ≈ 146). The rules on either side of it start at y ≈ 132, level with the other columns. So one column looks as if it came from a different template, and the shared top line across the row breaks. Gerstner (*Designing Programmes*): elements of one kind follow one set of rules. The fix: give all three columns the same top padding so their first lines align. Defect (it looks like a mistake). Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The copy is finished and careful. The British spellings are used consistently ("organisers", "programmes", "savoury"), there are no typos, and the details are concrete (the steps at four, the judges from the bakery, the farm shop and the allotment society), which give the event a real local voice worth keeping. The headline names the event plainly, so a first-time viewer can tell straight away that this announces a town festival.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I couldn't tell whether this is a finished poster or flyer, or a web page captured before images or styling loaded. That matters because the empty lower half and the missing picture could come from the capture. Check it in a live browser, or against the source file.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (colors, shapes, and directions carry the mood; each kind of element looks the same everywhere)

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies. One screen-sized page, 1280×800: a title over three columns of text.

**Findings**
None. All three lines are yes.

One finding has no checklist line, so I'm passing it to the director to place or drop:
1. *(No checklist line; this is my judgement.)* **The three events have no headings.** The page is clearly built as overview, then lantern walk (Saturday), then pie contest (Sunday), with one column each (x≈100–450, 478–806, 844–1173; text starts at y≈145). Nothing marks this middle level. A reader skimming for "when is the pie contest?" can't see that the third column is about it until they read the first sentence of each column. The only mention of the children's boat race is buried mid-sentence in column 1. Times and places are what readers act on (dusk at the town hall, entries by one o'clock, results at four), and they sit deep in running text. The piece has two levels (title, body) when its content has three. **Fix:** add a short heading to each column ("Lantern walk · Saturday at dusk", "Pie contest · Sunday afternoon"). Set it between the title and the body in size, or the same size as the body in bold, so it's a clear third level. Weight: **major**. The piece is useful only if people can find each event and its time, and right now they have to read everything to do that.

**What's working.**
- The title really does dominate. It's about twice the body size, bold, and in a darker ink than the body text, so the eye starts in the right place with no competition.
- Title and body differ in weight as well as size, and both use the same serif. This gives a calm, coherent two-step order that suits a community notice.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?** No. (**Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** No, for the same cause.) The middle column (x≈478–810) starts its first line at y≈150, while columns 1 and 3 start at y≈136. That is about 14 px, half of the ~28 px line pitch. Every line in the middle column therefore sits level with the gap between lines in its neighbours, all the way down: "On Saturday night…" sits between "The Harbour Lights festival returns to" and "the old market square…" on the left. The column rules all start at y≈132, so the top edge of that text block is also a near miss. It sits too close to read as a deliberate drop and too far off to read as aligned. When readers scan across the three columns, which is how a three-part notice like this gets compared, the rows don't line up. The page looks unfinished, as if a top margin or padding leaked into one column. Defect, and convention: Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid", says neighbouring columns share baselines and the first line stands at the top of the field. Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance", says an ambiguous placement makes the eye waver. Fix: remove whatever extra top space the middle column has (probably a stray margin on its first paragraph) so all three first lines share one baseline at y≈146 and the rest follow on the same line grid. Weight: major. This is the one thing that makes the layout look broken, and the fix is one value.
2. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** No (minor part). Text sits about 11 px to the right of each column rule (rule x≈467 to text x≈478, rule x≈833 to text x≈844). On the other side, the longest lines stop about 20–27 px before the next rule (column 1's longest line ends ≈446 against the rule at 467; column 2's ends ≈806 against the rule at 833). The rules look attached to the column on their right rather than splitting the gutter, and 11 px is tight beside 17 px body text. Taste. Fix: centre each rule in its gutter, or widen the gutter so the text has the same clear space on both sides of a rule. Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The grid itself is sound. Three equal columns, rules ~366 px apart, and the title's left edge (x=100) shares the first column's edge, so the page reads as one structure, left to right, with nothing leading the eye off it. The margins are generous and even (~100 px left, ~105 px right), and the empty space sits in one block below the text instead of being scattered between elements.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The ~330 px of empty space below the columns: the frame looks top-heavy, but it is most likely a short page captured in a 1280×800 viewport rather than a composition choice. Check the real page length. Also how the three columns reflow at narrower widths, and whether the middle column's offset survives there.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (exact alignment with no near-misses; baselines across columns).

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?** The first column ends on "seagulls." alone on its own last line (about x100–175, y440–465). That makes column 1 the longest of the three, so its bottom edge hangs one line below column 2's and two lines below column 3's. The single-word line reads as leftover rather than an ending, and it makes the uneven column feet stand out. This is the runt or widow problem Bringhurst warns about. Fix: rewrap so the last line holds at least two words, either by editing the copy (for example, trimming a word earlier in the paragraph) or with a non-breaking space or `text-wrap: pretty`. Convention, minor.

**What's working.**
- One serif family is used throughout: the bold display cut for the heading and the regular cut for the text. With big steps between the two sizes, the scale reads as two plain levels with nothing colliding.
- The narrow three-column measure (about 34–44 characters per line) has generous but not loose leading (about 28 px on about 19 px type) and near-black text on white. The paragraphs read comfortably and evenly.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Apostrophes in "children's" (column 1, about y257) and "o'clock" (column 3, about y341) may be straight rather than curly. They are too small to tell at this resolution, and I couldn't crop because the crop script was blocked. Check them in a zoomed crop or in the source.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 1 no (paragraphs and columns break cleanly), 1 unsure (curly quotes and true dashes)

**Walk (working notes)**

The image is about 1280×800, one screen, so I worked from the whole image. Running the crop script was refused (Bash isn't available in this mode).

First read: the eye lands on the bold headline "Harbour Lights festival" at the top left, then moves down into three columns of body text. It reads as a plain community notice, and it feels quiet and bookish. The whole piece is achromatic: near-black type, a white ground, and pale grey rules between the columns. No hues at all.

Job (my assumption): a web or print notice telling local residents what is happening at the festival.

Color:
- Small palette: yes. One neutral range only.
- Saturated colour kept to a small share of the area: yes. There is none.
- Clear range of light and dark that holds in grayscale: yes. Dark text on white, with the headline the heaviest mass.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. No temperature is used.
- Matching colours look the same everywhere: yes. The headline and body share one near-black.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colours used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning never carried by colour alone: yes. Nothing is colour-coded.
- Dark theme uses dark grey, not black: yes. It's a light theme.

No line was answered no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is fully achromatic (near-black, white, and light grey hairlines).

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** 
- The text looks like a softened near-black (a slightly cool dark grey) rather than pure #000 on white. That keeps strong contrast for body reading without the harsh glare of pure black on white. Keep it if a colour is added later.
- The column rules (at about x=467 and x=833, y=132–468) are a pale grey, much lighter than the type. They separate the columns without competing with the text, so the value structure stays type first, rules last.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes.

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photos, illustrations, icons, logos or marks, only a headline and three columns of text with thin vertical rules between them. I checked for a picture that failed to load, such as an empty box or a broken-image icon, and found none.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The middle column's text starts about 14 px lower (y ≈ 160) than the other two (y ≈ 145). That gap is too small to be an image slot that failed to load, so it isn't a pictures finding. It belongs to the arrangement critic. If the page is meant to have images, such as a lantern or harbour photo, check in a live browser that none of them failed to load.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped
